hook: Twenty-eight volunteers learned new words, half in short sessions spread over a week and half in one long cram. A week later the spaced group recalled 5.7 more words on average. How big is the real advantage? A two-sample t interval turns the two groups' means and spreads into a range of plausible values for the true difference.

chain.cause: The parameter is $\mu_1 - \mu_2$, the difference in true means
Estimating two standard deviations adds uncertainty
chain.effect: use $t^*$, with technology df (Welch) or the conservative df, the smaller of $n_1 - 1$ and $n_2 - 1$

chain.cause: Check random, 10% and normal/large sample for each group

ideas: Degrees of freedom: technology (Welch) gives a non-integer df; the conservative df is the smaller of $n_1 - 1$ and $n_2 - 1$, which gives a slightly wider interval. Both are accepted.
Conditions for each group: random (two independent random samples or random assignment), 10% (when sampling), normal/large sample.
Two independent groups use this interval; two linked measurements on each unit are paired and use a one-sample t interval on the differences.

misconception.wrong: Build a t interval for each group; if they overlap, there is no difference.
misconception.right: Two separate intervals answer a different question and can overlap even when the difference is clear. Estimate the difference directly with one two-sample t interval for $\mu_1 - \mu_2$.

summary: To estimate $\mu_1 - \mu_2$ from two independent samples or randomized groups, use $(\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2) \pm t^*\sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}$ with technology df or the conservative df. Check random, 10% and normal/large sample for each group, and interpret the interval as capturing the true difference in means, in the stated order.
